meta.title: Identification of Rare and Weak Signals with Machine Learning and Citizen Science: Planet Hunting with TESS and PLATO
meta.authorsHtml: Sofia Platymesi<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Suzanne Aigrain<sup>1</sup>, Chris Lintott<sup>1</sup>, Maximilian N. Günther<sup>2</sup>

abstract: Detecting rare and weak signals in vast astronomical datasets remains a central challenge in astronomy. Exoplanet discovery requires screening large datasets rich in confounding variability. We present a decision and prioritisation framework that combines machine learning with citizen science to identify such signals in data from the planet-hunting telescope, TESS. An ensemble comprising three complementary ResNet architectures is trained on over 1,000,000 labelled TESS lightcurves to emulate human decision-making. The system learns from human judgment, quantifies inter-model uncertainty, and uses this information to prioritise and escalate candidates. This human-AI framework preserves sensitivity to both standard planetary and atypical astrophysical signals while reducing the volume of data requiring human screening. Preliminary results show that the model recovered the same fraction of known objects of interest as the volunteer reviewers and reproduced 87% of their shortlisted targets. Inspection of the remaining 13% showed that the missed targets had been falsely flagged by volunteers and did not warrant follow-up, suggesting that the model has the potential to outperform human reviewers. We outline how this architecture can be extended from TESS to PLATO, arguing that uncertainty-aware, humancentred prioritisation systems offer a generalisable approach for future space-based survey operations.

blocks.html: Finding rare events and scientifically significant anomalies in large datasets is one of the greatest challenges of modern astronomy. NASA’s planet-hunting TESS mission (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has repeatedly observed more than 200,000 stars since 2018 [1], while ESA’s upcoming PLATO mission (PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of stars) is expected to collect tens of petabytes of data on nearly 300,000 stars over its mission lifetime [2]. The volume of data continues to grow, whereas expert time remains limited, making comprehensive manual screening increasingly impractical.

In the search for exoplanets, we face the additional challenge of detecting weak and infrequent signals in data often dominated by confounding effects such as stellar variability and instrumental systematics (e.g. scattered light and detector noise).

Automated pipelines are powerful but are inherently limited by the parameter space they are designed to explore. Although methods have been developed to detect both periodic and single events [3, 4], they remain optimised for predefined classes and are therefore less suited to recognising unusual or previously unseen phenomena. Citizen science complements these approaches by leveraging human pattern recognition and contextual interpretation to identify both expected planetary signals and unexpected astrophysical discoveries within large datasets (e.g. [5, 6]).

Recent advances in machine learning provide an opportunity to improve the review of large survey datasets while making more efficient use of human screening efforts. Here we combine citizen science and machine learning to develop a scalable hybrid framework by integrating machine learning into the long-standing Planet Hunters TESS (PHT) citizen science project, which has contributed significantly to exoplanet and broader astrophysical discoveries (e.g. [7, 8]). As a functional precursor to PLATO, TESS provides an ideal testbed for developing and evaluating a candidate prioritisation framework that can be adapted to future survey missions.

We first describe the existing PHT pipeline (Section 2.2), followed by the integration of machine learning into this workflow (Section 2.4). We then present preliminary results (Section 3) and conclude by discussing the framework’s performance, future development, and its potential application to PLATO (Section 4).

TESS has been surveying the sky since 2018, looking for exoplanets around nearby, bright stars [1]. It has detected thousands of planets and planetary candidates [9, 10] by observing how a star’s brightness dims as a planet passes in front of it, i.e. a transit event (e.g. Figure 1).

blocks.html: TESS observes a given field continuously for approximately a month, which makes up a sector of data. Each sector contains approximately 10,000 lightcurves (i.e. time series data encoding a star’s brightness changes over time), which has now led to a vast observational dataset.

The existing PHT pipeline starts with the volunteers visually inspecting data from a given TESS sector. Each lightcurve is seen by more than ten people and each of them highlights transit-like events in the data. Every target gets an aggregate score between 0 and 1, which reflects the volunteers’ confidence that this lightcurve contains a transit-like event.

From each sector, the 500 highest-scoring targets based on the volunteer consensus score are shortlisted for review by a subgroup of trained volunteers [7]. This vetting stage includes a series of diagnostic tests, such as examining background stars and pixel-level images during the event to verify that the signal originates from the target rather than a contaminating source.

Historically, this process has identified between one and five high-priority candidates per sector for followup. These include planetary candidates as well as stars exhibiting unusual or unexplained variability. Given that the process begins with more than 10,000 screened targets, this highlights the rarity of scientifically interesting events, i.e. a rate of only 0.01 - 0.05% of targets.

Our aim is to reduce the manual workload by identifying targets that can be safely excluded during the initial screening stage. To achieve this, we train a classification model to emulate volunteer decisions and evaluate whether it reproduces the same set of 500 shortlisted targets that progress to the second stage of review. If successful, the model can be integrated into the first stage of the pipeline, allowing volunteers to focus their efforts on targets with the greatest scientific potential. The resulting increase in efficiency will enable the systematic exploration of a much larger fraction of the TESS dataset, including background stars recorded in every observation through the Full Frame Images (FFIs), which so far have not been comprehensively inspected.

blocks.title: Improving the workflow with Machine Learning

blocks.html: Following promising results from earlier work [12] we now developed a framework comprised of three 1-D CNN architectures (Figure 2), adapted from [13] with residual connections as described in [14], trained, validated and tested on real, labelled data from PHT.

blocks.caption: Core CNN model architecture and its components. The three models are variations of this network.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: All three models take a 1D lightcurve data input (length=2700, single channel) and are based on residual convolutional layers. A ConvBlock consists of a 1Dconvolution, LeakyReLU activation (slope=0.01), dropout (p=0.1), optional max-pooling and batch normalisation. A ConvResBlock contains two ConvBlocks with a skip connection (Figure 2). The models largely share a core structure but their differences in kernel sizes and network depth make them sensitive to different features in the data (Table 1).

blocks.caption: Summary of CNN architectures and corresponding number of trainable parameters.
blocks.label: Table

blocks.html: Model A comprises 11 residual blocks. The first two use large kernels (k=65), without downsampling. Subsequent blocks downsample (pool=2) with decreasing kernel sizes (25→7→5→3) and increasing channels (1→64→128). This is followed by two dense blocks and a final linear layer with sigmoid activation.
Model B retains the same convolutional core but has a linear instead of dense output layer.
Model C has the same structure but uses smaller kernels (7→5→3) with growing channels (1→32→64→128) and a linear output layer.
All models are tuned with the same hyperparameters (Table 2).

All three models are trained on the same labelled dataset after some basic preprocessing (see [12]). We did not select any specific examples of planetary transits or known targets of interest (TOIs), as that would risk overfitting and missing atypical scientifically interesting signals, which citizen science has historically been successfully identifying (e.g. [15]). Similarly, no synthetic data were injected during model training. Instead, we used the entire labelled dataset available from the PHT project at the time, which included over 1,000,000 lightcurves from sectors 10 to 77, to train, validate and test the models, with an 80:10:10 split (Table 3).

blocks.alt: Data augmentation was applied in four ways:

blocks.html: lightcurves were mirrored; 10% of a lightcurve was randomly deleted; two sections of 25% of the lightcurve were shuffled and finally; lightcurves were injected data from another lightcurve with a volunteer score of 0.0 to simulate noise. Each augmentation type had an independent 10% chance of being applied to a given lightcurve during training. This created a more varied and realistic representations of the data and was found to improve performance.

A range of data splits and augmentation strategies were examined. This configuration was selected after multiple iterations because it provided the best balance between precision, recall, and retrieval of the 500 highest-scoring targets based solely on volunteer consensus scoring (as described in Section 2.2). The performance of each constituent model in its final iteration is shown in Table 4.

The proposed framework is novel in that it both learns the process of human decision-making and quantifies prediction uncertainty through inter-model disagreement. As the primary objective is to emulate the first stage of the PHT screening pipeline, volunteer labels are treated as ground truth during training, validation, and testing. To account for the fact that these labels are not exhaustive, model disagreement is explicitly incorporated as a measure of uncertainty (Section 2.5.2). Targets for which the models disagree are promoted for human review, allowing the framework to remain sensitive to ambiguous, unexpected, or potentially novel signals. The combined model therefore serves as an AI-assisted decision-support framework that both reproduces volunteer prioritisation and identifies targets for which a confident classification cannot be reached.
The aims of this framework are therefore twofold:
i) to emulate volunteer decision-making during the initial screening stage, thereby reducing the manual workload while preserving the scientific return of the pipeline; and
ii) to retain sensitivity to rare or scientifically interesting events, including signals that may not resemble typical planetary transits, by promoting uncertain candidates for human review.

Agreement Analysis The complete decision framework is illustrated in Figure 3. To maintain sensitivity to rare or atypical events, the final machine learning shortlist is constructed from the union of the three individual model shortlists. For comparison, we also retain the top 500 volunteerranked targets, allowing a direct comparison between the PHT and ML pipelines.

Uncertainty Representation The final shortlist additionally includes targets selected on the basis of model disagreement (Figure 3). These are identified after removing targets on which the models show strong agreement, thereby only highlighting candidates that would otherwise be excluded. Disagreement is quantified using both the coefficient of variation (CV = σ σ is the standard deviation and µ is the mean absolute score) and pairwise distances between model predictions (D = |m1 −m2| + |m2 −m3| + |m1 −m3|). Each uncertainty metric produces an independent shortlist of 100 candidates for human review.

As with the original PHT pipeline (see Section Section 2.2) the final target list is reviewed by the PHT science team and a subgroup of experienced and trained volunteers, who perform a series of vetting tests to this combined shortlist of targets. Targets that pass all these diagnostics are flagged to the community through public forums for follow-up observation (i.e. the final stage in Figure 3).

The framework was evaluated on TESS Sectors 78 and 79 using the three outlined shortlisting criteria: human review, model scores, and uncertainty representation. We compare the human-shortlisted targets with those selected by the combined model rankings and uncertainty metrics, and evaluate the fractional recovery of known targets relative to the original PHT pipeline. Table 5 summarises the progression from the full sector data set to the final vetted targets, while Figure 4 shows the fractional recovery rates for each sector.

blocks.caption: Workflow starting from a TESS sector of observations, going down the original PHT stream and the ML stream described in this work. They both feed into the Combined Shortlist of Targets to compare the two outputs. These targets are vetted by the science team and a team of trained volunteers. The targets that pass all the diagnostic tests during vetting are Candidates Flagged for follow-up and shared with the community through public forums.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The model predictions show strong agreement with human review, with shortlist overlaps of 89.2% in Sector 78 and 86.0% in Sector 79. It is worth highlighting that targets that were missed by the model failed initial diagnostic tests, indicating that they would not have progressed to follow-up observations and therefore were not of scientific interest.

The model also achieves a comparable recovery rate of previously identified TOIs and Threshold Crossing Events (TCEs, identified by TESS’s automated pipelines) to the original PHT pipeline in both sectors (∼50%; Table 5 and Figure 4). Recovery of known TOIs and TCEs provides a useful benchmark for comparison, however the primary objective is to identify scientifically interesting targets beyond those already detected by automated pipelines. Consequently, no complete ground-truth catalogue exists, and the final shortlisted candidates are also assessed through manual inspection.

Through that process we find that the framework also identified non-planetary but scientifically interesting systems. In Sector 78, a candidate multiple eclipsing stellar system (Figure 1, panel b) was shortlisted by both human reviewers and the model, demonstrating comparable decision-making beyond clear planetary signals. In Sector 79, one promising candidate (Figure 1, panel c) was identified only through its inter-model uncertainty score and not by human reviewers, highlighting the value of uncertainty representation. This candidate has passed the first-stage diagnostic tests and initial vetting. If confirmed, it could form part of a multi-planet system, as this star is already host to a TOI.

blocks.html: Figure 4 shows that the model recovers known TOIs and TCEs at comparable, and in some cases higher, rates than the volunteer-based ranking across similar review fractions. In the current PHT pipeline, the 500 highest-scoring targets are promoted for human review. At this review threshold, the recovery rates of the model and volunteer rankings are comparable, demonstrating that the model can reproduce the existing shortlisting process without a significant loss in recovery of scientifically interesting targets.

Beyond the recovery of known targets, the framework also recovered the two flagged for follow-up candidates discussed in Section 3 after substantially fewer targets had been reviewed than required by the human ranking alone. In Sector 78, the candidate was recovered after reviewing only the top 3% of targets (297 targets) using the combined model ranking, whereas the human inspection required the review of the top 4% (396 targets). This represents a 25% reduction in required review effort. In Sector 79, the uncertainty-based ranking placed the candidate within the top 2% (234 targets), while the volunteer ranking required review of the top 4% (468 targets), i.e. a 50% reduction in review effort.

While some stars do appear in repeated sectors, performance during inference is consistent with our baseline expectations, suggesting that the model generalises well. Future revisions of the training pipeline will explicitly account for overlapping observing cycles to eliminate any possibility of data leakage.

Preliminary results from Sector 80 are also promising with three possible planetary candidates identified: one of them was flagged by both the model and the volunteers and two of them were flagged only by the model and not by human consensus (Platymesi et al. in prep).

TESS remains in operation and, each month, in addition to its pre-selected target list, the mission acquires FFI (Full- Frame Image) observations containing photometric information for the many field stars captured within the same images. This expands the searchable stellar population from hundreds of thousands to millions of stars. Although several studies have demonstrated the feasibility of applying machine learning to these datasets (e.g., [16]), there is currently no systematic framework for screening and prioritising per sector FFI targets, i.e. the role that PHT has been fulfilling for the primary target catalogue.

In this work, we evaluated the proposed machine learning framework on the primary TESS target list and demonstrated that it can serve as an effective first-stage triage tool, substantially reducing the number of targets requiring manual inspection. This provides a practical route towards extending systematic screening to the much larger FFI catalogue, enabling the exploration of stellar populations that remain largely inaccessible to large-scale human vetting.

A scalable decision and prioritisation architecture will also be essential for PLATO, where increasingly large datasets must be balanced against limited expert time. Such a system must reliably rank planetary candidates while remaining sensitive to rare and atypical signals without overwhelming follow-up resources. Although demonstrated using TESS, the underlying framework is mission agnostic and can be adapted to future surveys through retraining on mission-specific data. More broadly, this work shows how computational methods and human expertise can operate in a feedback loop to effectively screen the next generation of exoplanet survey datastreams.

As TESS observations continue and preparations for PLATO advance, the framework will be extended through a more diverse ensemble of complementary model architectures, each optimised to capture different lightcurve characteristics, such as faint transit signals, irregular variability, or single-transit events. Combined model predictions, together with targets identified through high intermodel disagreement, will be presented to volunteers, whose classifications will be incorporated into an active learning framework. This iterative process will allow the models to improve as new labelled examples become available, following approaches successfully demonstrated in other citizen science projects (e.g. [17]).

The principal contribution of this work is in combining learnt human judgement, quantified inter-model uncertainty, and candidate prioritisation within a single decision framework. The results suggest that explicit uncertainty estimation will be particularly valuable for PLATO, where preserving sensitivity to rare events is as important as efficiently filtering routine candidates. Future developments will incorporate unsupervised anomaly detection to identify atypical or weak signals alongside transiting planets. By integrating anomaly detection into the prioritisation framework, the system will move beyond classification towards a unified decision-support architecture capable of identifying both expected planetary transits and previously unseen phenomena in future survey missions.
